questions.q: Why does a multi-team incident need a dedicated Incident Commander (IC), separate from the engineer actively debugging the problem?
options: Because the IC is always the most senior engineer and must personally approve every command run
Because debugging requires silence, and the IC's only job is to keep the incident channel quiet
So coordination and decision-making stay focused on running the incident, instead of competing for the same person's attention as the technical fix
Because company policy requires two people to be paged for every alert, regardless of severity
questions.explain: The IC owns the incident as a process — assigning work, deciding on escalation and trade-offs — specifically so that attention isn't split between coordinating the response and doing the hands-on technical fix.

questions.q: Which of the following is something an Incident Commander explicitly does NOT do?
options: Personally write the fix or run the rollback command
Decide which team is assigned to which part of the problem
Set the incident's severity level
Decide when to escalate to another team or wake up a director
questions.explain: The moment an IC starts doing hands-on technical work, they lose the ability to see the whole incident. The IC coordinates and decides; the responders do the technical fix.

questions.q: What is the main reason a Communications Lead is a separate role from the Incident Commander?
options: Communications Leads are junior staff who aren't trusted with technical decisions
So there is a single, consistent voice for anything leaving the incident channel, and the IC isn't interrupted answering the same question repeatedly
Because only the Communications Lead is allowed to speak to customers, by law
So the IC has someone to blame if the status page update is wrong
questions.explain: Without a dedicated owner, multiple people answer the same inbound question with slightly different information. A Communications Lead is the one point of contact, shielding the IC and responders from the firehose.

questions.q: What does the Scribe role capture during a live incident, and why does it matter?
options: Only the final root cause, written up after the incident is fully resolved
A list of which engineers were paged, for billing purposes
Screen recordings of every responder's terminal session
A live, timestamped timeline of hypotheses, mitigations, escalations, and status updates — which becomes the primary input to the postmortem
questions.explain: The Scribe keeps a continuous, timestamped log while the incident is live. That timeline is what the postmortem is built from, instead of reconstructing events days later from memory and scattered chat scrollback.

questions.q: How should the IC/Communications Lead/Scribe structure scale for a minor, single-team incident that one engineer resolves in ten minutes?
options: All three roles must still be staffed, even for a one-line config rollback
It shouldn't be used at all — the on-call engineer handles it solo, same as always; the full role structure is for incidents that grow past one team
A Deputy IC must always be assigned in addition to the primary IC
The Scribe role is replaced by an automated screen recording in every case
questions.explain: The roles exist so there's a known structure to step into once an incident grows past one team — a quick, single-team SEV3 doesn't need a Communications Lead or Scribe at all.
